body:
Follow-up to #5901 for #5891: it adopts the `get_number_value()` shape of `from_json(ArithmeticType&)` that #5901 left out because it made `GetArray<std::array<int, 1000>>` 2.4x slower. This PR finds the cause and fixes it.

## Why the shape mattered

- **vector/deque speedup.** `from_json(int&)` is inlined into every per-element loop. With one switch over four cases (boolean included), clang places the `boolean` test inside the hot compare chain. With `get_number_value()` plus a cold boolean path, the three number types (`value_t` 5–7) form the main path and the boolean moves behind a single `type <= 4` branch. This makes the vector loop 31% faster and the deque loop 12% faster.
- **std::array slowdown.** `get<std::array<T, N>>()` always takes the `identity_tag` overload (the `has_non_default_from_json` path), so it is never the `std::array<T, N>&` loop. That overload is the pack expansion `{ { j.at(Idx).template get<T>()... } }`. For N = 1000, clang emits one straight-line function of about 28,000 instructions: 1,000 inlined copies of the `at()` bounds and type checks plus the conversion. Its speed depends on how that ~110 KB body is inlined and laid out, not on the conversion itself. The pinned-alignment base build alone moves it from 657 to 957 ns, so any change to `from_json(int&)` shows up there 1,000 times.

## Change

- `from_json(ArithmeticType&)` uses `get_number_value()`, then accepts a boolean on a cold path. `get_arithmetic_value()` still rejects booleans.
- New `from_json_std_array()`: it checks the size once and reads the inner array directly instead of calling `at(i)` per element. Both `std::array` paths use it:
  - `from_json(j, std::array<T, N>&)` (`get_to`), for all `T`;
  - `from_json(j, identity_tag<std::array<T, N>>)` (`get`), when `T` is trivial (`std::is_trivial`, or the two `is_trivially_*` traits in C++26, as in `binary_writer`). A trivial type can't tell default construction plus assignment from construction in place. Non-trivial and non-default-constructible element types keep the pack expansion.
- Codegen with Apple clang 21 at `-O3` on a probe TU: `from_json(identity_tag<std::array<int, 1000>>)` drops from about 28,000 instructions (1,000 `throw_array_index_out_of_range` and 986 `throw_type_must_be` call sites) to 49.

Behaviour is unchanged. Elements are still converted in order, so a type error in an earlier element is still reported before a missing element. A short array still throws `out_of_range.401` for the first missing index (via `j.at(size)`), and longer arrays and booleans convert as before. New tests in `unit-constructor1.cpp` cover these cases and also pass against the #5901 head.

## Benchmarks

Apple M-series, Apple clang 21, `-O3 -flto`, Google Benchmark 1.10.0, `tests/benchmarks`. Base is the #5901 head (0e5a906cd). Each binary ran 4 rounds of 5 repetitions with random interleaving, and the two binaries alternated in random order per round. Values are medians of 20 runs, relative to base.

| benchmark | base | `get_number_value` only | `std::array` loop only | this PR | this PR, alignment-pinned¹ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GetArray<std::vector<int>> | 1005 ns | −31.5% | −0.1% | **−31.5%** | **−31.7%** |
| GetArray<std::deque<int>> | 1355 ns | −12.0% | +0.1% | **−11.6%** | **−12.2%** |
| GetArray<std::array<int, 1000>> | 657 ns | **+138.6%** | +0.2% | −0.2% | **−31.7%** |
| GetArray<std::set<int>> | 41.9 µs | +1.0% | +0.8% | +1.3% | +1.3%² |
| GetVectorInt/signed_ints | 3.50 ms | | | +1.4% | +0.4% |
| GetVectorDouble/floats | 0.69 ms | | | +1.7% | +0.5% |
| GetMap/citm_catalog | 2.52 ms | | | +1.9% | +0.5% |
| ToJsonStrings/copy | 5.95 ms | | | +1.2% | +0.4% |
| ToJsonStrings/move | 3.26 ms | | | +2.1% | +0.4% |
| ParseString/canada | 5.61 ms | | | +1.7% | +1.1%² |
| ParseString/citm_catalog | 2.01 ms | | | +0.7% | +1.2%² |
| ParseString/twitter | 1.10 ms | | | +3.5% | +0.4% |
| ParseString/floats | 31.9 ms | | | +3.6% | +0.1% |
| ParseString/jeopardy | 133 ms | | | +2.5% | −0.8% |
| ParseString/signed_ints | 33.1 ms | | | +0.8% | +0.1% |
| ParseString/unsigned_ints | 31.4 ms | | | +0.7% | +0.6% |
| ParseString/small_signed_ints | 23.3 ms | | | +1.6% | −0.2% |
| ParseStringOrdered/canada | 5.62 ms | | | +0.3% | +2.4%² |
| ParseStringOrdered/citm_catalog | 2.25 ms | | | −0.8% | −1.1% |
| ParseStringOrdered/twitter | 1.12 ms | | | +0.9% | −0.2% |
| ParseStringOrdered/jeopardy | 137 ms | | | +0.6% | −0.3% |

¹ `-falign-functions=64 -mllvm -align-all-functions=6 -mllvm -align-all-nofallthru-blocks=6`, passed to the compiler and the LTO link (every function starts on a 64-byte boundary).

² Rows that are not touched by this change and stay above +1% only in wall-clock time. In the unpinned build, the parser and lexer functions are byte-for-byte the same size in both binaries and just shifted by 0x90 bytes. With pinned alignment, `/usr/bin/time -l` shows the same retired instructions and cycles for ParseString/canada and ParseStringOrdered/canada (cycles +0.1%). For GetArray<std::set<int>> the new code retires 0.3% fewer instructions at the same cycles.

## Breaking changes

None. No public API or behaviour changes. The new helpers are in `nlohmann::detail`.

+    using is_trivial_element = conjunction<std::is_trivially_copyable<T>, std::is_trivially_default_constructible<T>>;

review_comments.body:
Yes. The trigger is our `--indent-preproc-block` option: astyle indents everything inside an `#ifdef` block at namespace level, so two aliases inside `#ifdef`/`#else` always get pushed in. `is_trivial_element` is now a struct, and the `#ifdef` only picks its base (`conjunction<std::is_trivially_copyable<T>, std::is_trivially_default_constructible<T>>` or `std::is_trivial<T>`), which astyle leaves at column 0. Fixed in `469e29334`.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

Right, I misread which function you meant. The trigger is astyle's default `--max-continuation-indent=40`: the `(` of `std::array<T, N> from_json_inplace_array(` was in column 41, so astyle falls back to a plain double indent for the continuation lines instead of aligning them. Fixed in `cf4e0164c` by renaming the function to `from_json_make_array`, which keeps the parenthesis within the limit, so both overloads now align normally.
